[00:00] Morgan: hey thanks everyone for jumping on, um we're excited to chat through your serving plans and uh figure out migration blockers. can you do quick intros?
[00:15] Aisha: yeah sure i'm aisha head of ml at summit data we run most of our training infra in house and for serving we've been using vLLM plus a little TGI for some models and then fronting openai for a few safety sensitive flows.
[00:30] Tom: tom platform eng, i manage k8s clusters, network and we handle scaling for inference today.
[00:35] Priya: priya security, i'll be looking at data residency and key management stuff.
[00:40] Morgan: great thanks, ravi quick note?
[00:45] Ravi: hi all, ravi se here, i'll dig into the compatibility and performance side, especially kv cache behavior and batching differences.
[00:52] Aisha: high level we want similar latency to our vLLM routes, cost improvements if possible and definitely no regressions in output. evaluation parity is a must.
[01:10] Morgan: makes sense, when you say vLLM routes can you quantify typical p50/p95 and token mixes?
[01:20] Aisha: p50 is ~60ms on our 8k context models, p95 around 160ms, token mix is roughly 70% short autosummary queries (20-50 tokens) and 30% long generations (800-2k tokens).
[01:40] Tom: and our infra topology is mixed, some on-prem GPUs (A100) and some cloud VMs on Azure, we use TGI as a wrapper for routing to different backends.
[02:05] Ravi: ok so interesting. two things pop out: 1) sequence length distribution will affect kernel selection and batching on Redwood runtime, 2) if you rely on TGI-specific tokenization adapters that might be a small porting work.
[02:20] Aisha: yeah tokenization—we do a few weird pre-tokenization steps for consistent evals. will that break?
[02:30] Ravi: probably not break but we need to validate token alignment. i've seen off-by-one mismatches when switching runtimes, especially with custom merges. we'll add that to the checklist.
[02:50] Priya: on security, what are your options for private deployments? we need to know if we can run the private control plane in our VPC and keep KMS keys internal.
[03:05] Morgan: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed control plane and VPC peering, we can integrate with customer KMS or HSM, there are some enterprise packaging items. we'd share the on-prem checklist.
[03:25] Priya: do you support bring-your-own-HSM?
[03:30] Ravi: we do integrations commonly with AWS KMS and external HSMs via standard KMIP, but exact process depends on deployment model. we'll need details about your HSM vendor.
[03:45] Aisha: another big one is eval parity — we have a 3k prompt benchmark suite and if outputs change we fail. how do you help ensure parity with our baseline?
[04:00] Morgan: good question. we typically run parity checks at model onboarding: tokenization validation, output diffs on your eval set, and a regression alerting pipeline. also can do controlled rollouts and compare perplexity / ROUGE etc.
[04:20] Aisha: do you rerun evals automatically on quantized models? we use q4 to save cost currently.
[04:30] Ravi: our Optimize tool suggests quant profiles per workload; we do quality monitoring and flag regressions. quantization can change outputs, so we recommend an eval pass and optional canary to ensure acceptable delta.
[04:50] Tom: latency is huge. how does Redwood hitting p95 compare to our vLLM tail?
[05:05] Ravi: depends on deployment: hosted may have extra network hop but is tuned for latency. Dedicated on-prem GPUs or Redwood Private in your VPC is closest to your current p95. we can provide benchmark numbers for similar hardware; we'll propose a latency SLO and run a benchmark with your traces.
[05:30] Aisha: network egress cost is another factor—if we route to hosted that adds egress and costs.
[05:40] Morgan: yep we'd model egress in the cost calculator. Dedicated pools can live in cloud regions to minimize cross-region egress, Private avoids vendor egress.
[05:55] Priya: audit logs and data retention — we need full request-level logs for a 13-month retention and strict RBAC. does Redwood support that?
[06:05] Morgan: yes, Redwood Console supports token-level traceability, per-route dashboards, and configurable retention in enterprise plans. RBAC and SSO/SAML are available. we can share the security pack.
[06:20] Aisha: about function calling and structured outputs — we're using that heavily, any compatibility notes?
[06:30] Ravi: function-calling patterns are supported; the main porting work is ensuring the schema and response parsing are unchanged. streaming behaviors can differ slightly, but we have streaming APIs.
[06:50] Tom: we use hybrid routing today — lower-cost models handle most inference, then fallback to a larger model for hard cases. can Redwood support smart routing?
[07:00] Morgan: absolutely, smart routing by policy (latency vs cost) is core: you can set routing rules, automatic fallback to compatible model variants and even region-based routing.
[07:20] Aisha: compatibility with Hugging Face formats? we have some HF transformers forks in house.
[07:30] Ravi: we support HF model artifacts as long as weights and config are standard; custom ops might need build steps. for TGI and vLLM there are known patterns; we'll run a quick compatibility scan.
[08:00] Morgan: to help scope a pilot — what's your most critical workload to migrate first?
[08:10] Aisha: our summarization route, high-volume short-context, it's the cheapest place to get wins on cost and latency.
[08:20] Morgan: good, that maps well to Redwood's batching/caching improvements—prefix/KV caching can reduce token cost on repeated contexts.
[08:35] Tom: what's the typical pilot duration and what do we get?
[08:40] Morgan: a 4-week pilot usually: benchmarking, model onboarding, tokenization checks, and a small canary to compare production outputs. price credits often included depending on scope.
[09:00] Priya: legal — we have to run a security questionnaire. do you have a SOC2 report and standard security docs?
[09:10] Morgan: yes SOC2 Type II, ISO is in progress, and we have a security packet. we'll send the link and an NDA redline if needed.
[09:25] Aisha: one squishy concern: we've got some custom inference hooks in TGI — can those be reproduced?
[09:35] Ravi: maybe; we'd need to see the hooks. sometimes hooks can be replaced by Redwood middleware or by adapting the model runner. it's on our compatibility list.
[09:50] Tom: about autoscaling — we need predictable throughput for batch windows, can Redwood handle bursty traffic?
[10:00] Morgan: Dedicated pools have configurable autoscaling and burst capacity. Private gives you full control of scaling policies too. we can discuss commit tiers.
[10:15] Aisha: what's the onboarding time to go live for a single model? rough estimate.
[10:20] Ravi: model onboarding for a standard HF model is often 3-7 days for testing and validations; if there are custom ops or quantization steps it can extend to 2-3 weeks.
[10:40] Priya: for KMS integration timeline?
[10:45] Morgan: depends on the vendor, but initial integration and key material exchange can be 1-2 weeks with standard KMS; HSM might add time.
[11:00] Aisha: ok can you run a short risk list now for our migration?
[11:10] Ravi: sure: 1) tokenization mismatch (easy to detect but must be validated), 2) custom TGI hooks and op compatibility (could be moderate effort), 3) quantization/regression risks (need evals), 4) networking/egress constraints for hosted, 5) SLA and any dedicated sizing mismatches.
[11:35] Tom: anything else about eval parity methodology?
[11:40] Morgan: we use your eval suite, run a diff across outputs, measure BLEU/ROUGE/perplexity depending on use case, and flag regression thresholds you set. can show tooling.
[12:00] Aisha: ok if we do pilot, we want a gating metric: no more than 2% drop in our key quality metric and p95 latency within 20% of baseline.
[12:12] Morgan: understood, we'll align on thresholds and capture them in the pilot SOW.
[12:30] Ravi: one technical note—vLLM and Redwood handle KV cache differently; if you have long conversational traces we need to ensure cache warming and eviction patterns match your current behavior.
[12:50] Aisha: good point, our long sessions are important for context.
[13:03] Tom: what about model version pinning and rollouts? we do a lot of canary tests.
[13:10] Morgan: Redwood supports model versioning, canaries, A/B and automatic fallback policies — we can align on rollout windows.
[13:35] Priya: what's the data retention for request logs in Private vs Hosted?
[13:45] Morgan: Hosted: configurable but retention is managed by Redwood (enterprise plans allow longer retention). Private: you control retention. we'll send the retention matrix.
[14:00] Aisha: regarding cost, any quick back-of-envelope for moving heavy short-context volume to Redwood hosted?
[14:10] Morgan: need sample traces but usually cost per token plus possible committed throughput. Dedicated often reduces unit cost for high volume. we'll run a cost model once we have traces.
[14:35] Ravi: also caching can reduce upstream tokens; if you have repeated prefixes we can save a lot.
[15:00] Aisha: ok let's talk timelines, we want pilot in next month if possible.
[15:08] Morgan: we can aim for pilot kickoff week of 2026-05-25 pending docs and traces.
[15:20] Tom: i'll need internal signoff for network peering and budget.
[15:25] Priya: legal will look at security pack and then we can expedite.

[31:00] Aisha: will you support our custom token merges during tokenization? we've got pre-tokenized embeddings pipeline.
[31:15] Ravi: yes we can accept pre-tokenized payloads in some paths, but we should test that in the pilot to ensure embeddings align.

[35:10] Morgan: hosted uses a range list we publish; Dedicated uses customer-dedicated infrastructure; Private avoids egress. we'll share precise ranges.

[38:12] Morgan: yes we have references in fintech and regulated healthcare under NDAs; we'll coordinate an intro if helpful.

[40:12] Morgan: yes, from Redwood: pricing + pilot SLA, compatibility scan (Ravi), benchmark plan, and security pack.
